title: AI and the Living Word: Education's Homecoming
author: Wegerif, Rupert
summary: Rupert Wegerif uses Plato's Phaedrus and Homer's Odyssey as lenses for thinking about what AI can and cannot do in education. Plato's critique of writing—that it cannot respond to the individual questioner, cannot explain itself, repeats the same thing forever—applies equally to AI that produces outputs without genuine dialogue. Wegerif argues that education's purpose is not to produce knowledge-reproducers but to help students enter the living conversation: encountering other voices, making judgements, taking responsibility, and learning to answer for what they say.
points: Plato's critique of written words as painted figures that remain silently fixed when questioned applies equally to AI that generates text without genuine responsiveness to the individual before it.
The 'living word of knowledge' is not about speech versus writing but about whether language is taken up in a genuine act of response—writing can be alive and speech can be dead.
Reading is not the transfer of information from page to memory but the taking up of what is written into one's own conception—something AI can replicate the surface of but not the substance.
Education produces people who sound knowledgeable by reproducing what's written without necessarily knowing how to respond to a person, a new situation, or an unanticipated question.
Homer's Odyssey is the great homecoming story: we return home changed by the journey, as someone else—education should produce the same transformation, not mere data acquisition.
The goal of education is to help people enter the conversation: to encounter other voices, make judgements, take responsibility, and discover possibilities through genuine dialogue.
quotes: We forget how to step inside again: to take what we have learned back into the living weave of our projects and relationships, until it becomes not merely an object we look at but a way of seeing and acting, and the ground for the next step forward.

Reading is then not the transfer of information from page to memory, something that AI can do rather better than I can, but it is the taking up of what is written into my own concerns and projects, letting it question me and letting it matter.

Phaedrus responds: “You mean the living word of knowledge which has a soul, and of which the written word is properly no more than an image?” The difference Socrates is pointing to runs deeper than the technology of writing.

Education can produce people who sound knowledgeable because they can reproduce what has been written, without necessarily knowing how to respond to another person, to a new situation or to the world itself.

We answer not only to a teacher, an employer or another individual, but to the larger horizon behind them: to other people, to the living world, to the future and to everything that has not yet been decided.
It is to help people enter the conversation: to encounter other voices, make judgements, take responsibility, discover possibilities and learn how to answer for what they say and what they do.
